claim: Excessive consumption of sucrose has been implicated in the pathogenesis of metabolic dysfunction‐associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD) and other related metabolic syndromes.
source: Excessive consumption of sucrose, in the form of sugar-sweetened beverages, has been implicated in the pathogenesis of metabolic dysfunction‐associated fatty liver disease (MAFLD) and other related metabolic syndromes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to existing literature and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) pathway plays a crucial role in response to dietary stressors.
source: The c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) pathway plays a crucial role in response to dietary stressors, and it was demonstrated that the inhibition of the JNK pathway could potentially be used in the treatment of MAFLD.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior research demonstrating JNK's role in dietary stress response.

claim: Inhibition of the JNK pathway could potentially be used in the treatment of MAFLD.
source: The c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) pathway plays a crucial role in response to dietary stressors, and it was demonstrated that the inhibition of the JNK pathway could potentially be used in the treatment of MAFLD.
evidence: This claim is supported by prior demonstrations cited in the manuscript.

claim: JNK inhibition by JNK-IN-5A effectively reduces circulating triglyceride accumulation in rats subjected to sucrose consumption.
source: Our data demonstrate that JNK inhibition by JNK-IN-5A effectively reduces the circulating triglyceride accumulation and inflammation in rats subjected to sucrose consumption.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the study, including plasma triglyceride measurements shown in Figure 2b.

claim: JNK inhibition by JNK-IN-5A effectively reduces inflammation in rats subjected to sucrose consumption.
source: Our data demonstrate that JNK inhibition by JNK-IN-5A effectively reduces the circulating triglyceride accumulation and inflammation in rats subjected to sucrose consumption.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced LDH levels (an inflammation marker) in treated rats.

claim: Sucrose overconsumption primarily induces transcriptional dysfunction related to fatty acid metabolism in the liver and adipose tissues.
source: Coexpression analysis and genome-scale metabolic modeling reveal that sucrose overconsumption primarily induces transcriptional dysfunction related to fatty acid and oxidative metabolism in the liver and adipose tissues, which are largely rectified after JNK inhibition at a clinically relevant dose.
evidence: This claim is supported by coexpression analysis and genome-scale metabolic modeling performed in the study.

claim: Sucrose overconsumption primarily induces transcriptional dysfunction related to oxidative metabolism in the liver and adipose tissues.
source: Coexpression analysis and genome-scale metabolic modeling reveal that sucrose overconsumption primarily induces transcriptional dysfunction related to fatty acid and oxidative metabolism in the liver and adipose tissues, which are largely rectified after JNK inhibition at a clinically relevant dose.
evidence: This claim is supported by coexpression analysis and genome-scale metabolic modeling performed in the study.

claim: Transcriptional dysfunction induced by sucrose overconsumption in liver and adipose tissues is largely rectified after JNK inhibition at a clinically relevant dose.
source: Coexpression analysis and genome-scale metabolic modeling reveal that sucrose overconsumption primarily induces transcriptional dysfunction related to fatty acid and oxidative metabolism in the liver and adipose tissues, which are largely rectified after JNK inhibition at a clinically relevant dose.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptomic data showing reversal of gene expression patterns after JNK-IN-5A treatment.

claim: Skeletal muscle exhibited minimal transcriptional changes to sucrose overconsumption.
source: Skeletal muscle exhibited minimal transcriptional changes to sucrose overconsumption but underwent substantial metabolic adaptation following the JNK inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis showing only 257 DEGs (1.3%) in skeletal muscle in response to sucrose.

claim: Skeletal muscle underwent substantial metabolic adaptation following JNK inhibition.
source: Skeletal muscle exhibited minimal transcriptional changes to sucrose overconsumption but underwent substantial metabolic adaptation following the JNK inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptomic data showing 4,159 DEGs (20.9%) in skeletal muscle after JNK_D1 treatment.

claim: Extrahepatic metabolism plays a critical role in the development of diet-induced steatosis.
source: Furthermore, our findings underpin the critical role of extrahepatic metabolism in the development of diet-induced steatosis, offering valuable guidance for future studies focused on JNK-targeting for effective treatment of MAFLD.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the multi-tissue transcriptomic analysis showing significant changes in adipose tissue and skeletal muscle.

claim: The global prevalence of MAFLD is estimated to be 20–25%.
source: The global prevalence of MAFLD is estimated to be 20–25% (Younossi et al., 2023), and it is rapidly increasing in parallel with the epidemic of obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus (Kotsiliti, 2023; Le et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Younossi et al., 2023.

claim: MAFLD prevalence is rapidly increasing in parallel with the epidemic of obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus.
source: The global prevalence of MAFLD is estimated to be 20–25% (Younossi et al., 2023), and it is rapidly increasing in parallel with the epidemic of obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus (Kotsiliti, 2023; Le et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kotsiliti, 2023 and Le et al., 2023.

claim: There is an absence of approved pharmacological therapy for MAFLD by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA).
source: Given the absence of approved pharmacological therapy for MAFLD by the US Food and Drug Treatment (FDA) (Llovet et al., 2023; Nassir et al., 2015), the discovery and development of effective therapies are of great importance in MAFLD treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Llovet et al., 2023 and Nassir et al., 2015.

claim: Rats subjected to a 12 week high-sucrose diet (25% w/v sucrose) developed a metabolic syndrome phenotype characterized by glucose intolerance, hepatic steatosis, and insulin resistance.
source: For instance, a previous study reported that rats subjected to a 12 wk high-sucrose diet (25% w/v sucrose), developed a metabolic syndrome phenotype characterized by glucose intolerance, HS, and insulin resistance (IR) (Sousa et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sousa et al., 2018.

claim: Consumption of sucrose at a concentration of 10% w/v can disrupt energy balance and induce hepatic steatosis within 10–20 weeks.
source: Recent research further reveals that the consumption of sucrose at a concentration of 10% w/v can disrupt energy balance and induce HS within 10–20 wk (Jang et al., 2020; Stephenson et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jang et al., 2020 and Stephenson et al., 2022.

claim: JNK has three isoforms: JNK1 and JNK2, which are ubiquitously expressed, and JNK3 is specifically expressed in the brain, testis, and heart.
source: JNK has three isoforms: JNK1 and JNK2, which are ubiquitously expressed, and JNK3 is specifically expressed in the brain, testis, and heart (Chang and Karin, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chang and Karin, 2001.

claim: MCD diet-fed JNK1 null mice exhibited significantly reduced levels of key hallmarks of MAFLD, including hepatic steatosis, TG accumulation, inflammation, lipid peroxidation, hepatocyte injury, and apoptosis.
source: Notably, MCD diet-fed JNK1 null mice exhibited significantly reduced levels of key hallmarks of MAFLD, including HS, TG accumulation, inflammation, lipid peroxidation, hepatocyte injury, and apoptosis (Singh et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Singh et al., 2009.

claim: High-fat diet-fed mice with hepatic ablation of both JNK1 and JNK2 are protected from hepatic steatosis and insulin resistance.
source: Similarly, high-fat diet-fed mice with hepatic ablation of both JNK1 and JNK2 are protected from HS and IR (Vernia et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Vernia et al., 2014.

claim: JNK-IN-5A is a selective JNK2 and JNK3 inhibitor.
source: Moreover, our previous study demonstrated that JNK-IN-5A, a selective JNK2 and JNK3 inhibitor (Angell et al., 2007; Cerbone et al., 2012), effectively decreased fat accumulation and steatosis-related protein expression in an in vitro steatosis model (Kim et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Angell et al., 2007 and Cerbone et al., 2012.

claim: JNK-IN-5A effectively decreased fat accumulation and steatosis-related protein expression in an in vitro steatosis model.
source: Moreover, our previous study demonstrated that JNK-IN-5A, a selective JNK2 and JNK3 inhibitor (Angell et al., 2007; Cerbone et al., 2012), effectively decreased fat accumulation and steatosis-related protein expression in an in vitro steatosis model (Kim et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2023, which is the authors' previous study.

claim: None of the administered doses of JNK-IN-5A led to significant changes in body weight and hematological parameters in rats.
source: We observed none of the administrated doses led to significant changes in body weight and hematological parameters (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the 7-day oral toxicology study.

claim: The two higher doses of JNK-IN-5A decreased the levels of sodium in female rats.
source: In addition, the two higher doses of JNK-IN-5A decreased the levels of sodium in female rats and elevated the level of phosphate in both sexes (Figure 2a, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical chemistry data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The two higher doses of JNK-IN-5A elevated the level of phosphate in both sexes of rats.
source: In addition, the two higher doses of JNK-IN-5A decreased the levels of sodium in female rats and elevated the level of phosphate in both sexes (Figure 2a, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by clinical chemistry data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The administration of JNK-IN-5A is well tolerated with regard to adverse clinical signs, body weight, and clinical hematology parameters.
source: Overall, the administration of JNK-IN-5A is well tolerated with regard to adverse clinical signs, body weight, and clinical hematology parameters.
evidence: This claim is supported by the toxicology study data showing no significant adverse effects.

claim: Liquid sucrose consumption resulted in significantly increased plasma levels of triglycerides compared to healthy controls.
source: We observed that liquid sucrose consumption resulted in significantly increased plasma levels of TG (p<0.0001) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH, p<0.0001), which is an inflammation marker, compared to the healthy controls (Figure 2b, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by plasma biochemistry measurements shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Liquid sucrose consumption resulted in significantly increased plasma levels of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), an inflammation marker, compared to healthy controls.
source: We observed that liquid sucrose consumption resulted in significantly increased plasma levels of TG (p<0.0001) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH, p<0.0001), which is an inflammation marker, compared to the healthy controls (Figure 2b, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by plasma biochemistry measurements shown in Figure 2b.

claim: JNK-IN-5A-treated rats on sucrose water exhibited significantly lower levels of triglycerides compared to sucrose-only controls.
source: On sucrose water, JNK-IN-5A-treated rats exhibited significantly lower levels of TG (JNK_D1, p<0.0001; JNK_D2, p<0.001), aspartate aminotransferase (AST; JNK_D1, p=0.09; JNK_D2, p=0.005), and LDH (JNK_D1, n.s.; JNK_D2, p=0.015) but had no significant change on body weight, glucose, high-density lipoprotein (HDL) and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) as compared to their corresponding controls (Figure 2b, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by plasma biochemistry measurements shown in Figure 2b.

claim: JNK-IN-5A-treated rats on sucrose water exhibited significantly lower levels of aspartate aminotransferase (AST) compared to sucrose-only controls.
source: On sucrose water, JNK-IN-5A-treated rats exhibited significantly lower levels of TG (JNK_D1, p<0.0001; JNK_D2, p<0.001), aspartate aminotransferase (AST; JNK_D1, p=0.09; JNK_D2, p=0.005), and LDH (JNK_D1, n.s.; JNK_D2, p=0.015) but had no significant change on body weight, glucose, high-density lipoprotein (HDL) and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) as compared to their corresponding controls (Figure 2b, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by plasma biochemistry measurements shown in Figure 2b.

claim: JNK-IN-5A-treated rats on sucrose water exhibited significantly lower levels of LDH compared to sucrose-only controls.
source: On sucrose water, JNK-IN-5A-treated rats exhibited significantly lower levels of TG (JNK_D1, p<0.0001; JNK_D2, p<0.001), aspartate aminotransferase (AST; JNK_D1, p=0.09; JNK_D2, p=0.005), and LDH (JNK_D1, n.s.; JNK_D2, p=0.015) but had no significant change on body weight, glucose, high-density lipoprotein (HDL) and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) as compared to their corresponding controls (Figure 2b, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by plasma biochemistry measurements shown in Figure 2b.

claim: JNK-IN-5A-treated rats exhibit no evidence of anxiety and behavior disorders.
source: Collectively, the behavior tests indicate the JNK-IN-5A-treated rats exhibit no evidence of anxiety and behavior disorders.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data including passive avoidance test, locomotor activity test, and elevated plus maze test.

claim: Mapk8 and Mapk9 have high expression in liver, vWAT, SkM, and brain tissues.
source: As anticipated, Mapk8 and Mapk9 have high expression in all these tissues (liver, vWAT, SkM, and brain) whereas Mapk10 is highly expressed specifically in the brain tissue (Figure 2c, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Mapk10 is highly expressed specifically in the brain tissue.
source: As anticipated, Mapk8 and Mapk9 have high expression in all these tissues (liver, vWAT, SkM, and brain) whereas Mapk10 is highly expressed specifically in the brain tissue (Figure 2c, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Treatment of JNK_D1 effectively alleviated the JNK1 gene expression in the liver.
source: Our analysis indicates that the treatment of JNK_D1 effectively alleviated the JNK1 gene expression in the liver (padj = 0.03) and exerted more profound inhibitory effects on both JNK1 (padj = 0.0009) and JNK2 gene expression (padj = 2.2e-07) in SkM (Figure 2c, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Treatment of JNK_D1 exerted profound inhibitory effects on both JNK1 and JNK2 gene expression in skeletal muscle.
source: Our analysis indicates that the treatment of JNK_D1 effectively alleviated the JNK1 gene expression in the liver (padj = 0.03) and exerted more profound inhibitory effects on both JNK1 (padj = 0.0009) and JNK2 gene expression (padj = 2.2e-07) in SkM (Figure 2c, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Plasma TG level is significantly correlated with the JNK2 gene expression in skeletal muscle.
source: Interestingly, we found that plasma TG level is significantly correlated with the JNK2 gene expression in SkM (Figure 2d and e).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2d and e.

claim: Liquid sucrose ingestion resulted in the largest transcriptional changes in the liver and vWAT.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) revealed that liquid sucrose ingestion resulted in the largest transcriptional changes in the liver and vWAT (Figure 3a), which is consistent with previous results (Stephenson et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 3a and is consistent with cited previous results.

claim: JNK-IN-5A treatment corrected to a large extent the gene expression profile in the liver and vWAT of treated-rats towards the profile of healthy controls.
source: Of note, we observed that JNK-IN-5A treatment, especially JNK_D1, corrected to a large extent of the gene expression profile in the liver and vWAT of treated-rats towards the profile of healthy controls on a principal components space (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The liver had the largest number of differentially expressed genes associated with liquid sucrose ingestion, comprising a total of 2771 DEGs (14%).
source: In parallel with the results presented above, differential gene expression analysis revealed that the liver had the largest number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs, DESeq2-Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p<0.01) associated with liquid sucrose ingestion, comprising a total of 2771 DEGs (14%), followed closely by vWAT with 2,724 DEGs (13.8%), SkM with 257 DEGs (1.3%), and the brain with a modest 30 DEGs (0.2%) (Figure 3b and c, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b–e, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3b and c.

claim: JNK_D1 treatment substantially suppressed the expression of 60.7% of sucrose-induced DEGs in the liver.
source: Specifically, in the liver, JNK_D1 treatment substantially suppressed the expression of 60.7% (1143 out of 1884, hypergeometric p≈ 0) sucrose-induced DEGs and elevated the expression of 22% of sucrose-repressed genes (195 out of 887, hypergeometric p=6.9e-129) (Figure 3d, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis and hypergeometric testing shown in Figure 3d.

claim: JNK_D1 treatment elevated the expression of 22% of sucrose-repressed genes in the liver.
source: Specifically, in the liver, JNK_D1 treatment substantially suppressed the expression of 60.7% (1143 out of 1884, hypergeometric p≈ 0) sucrose-induced DEGs and elevated the expression of 22% of sucrose-repressed genes (195 out of 887, hypergeometric p=6.9e-129) (Figure 3d, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis and hypergeometric testing shown in Figure 3d.

claim: JNK_D1 treatment reversed 42.2% and 31.4% of DEGs in vWAT.
source: Likewise, we observed a reversal of 42.2% and 31.4% (698 of 1655 and 336 out of 1069, respectively) DEGs in vWAT (Figure 3d, Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Pathway enrichment analysis of JNK_D1 reversed genes identified significantly enriched KEGG pathways related to carbon metabolism, fatty acid metabolism, protein processing in ER, and oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Pathway enrichment analysis of JNK_D1 reversed genes identified significantly enriched KEGG pathways related to carbon metabolism, fatty acid metabolism, protein processing in ER, and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) (Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p<0.01) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c and d).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2c and d.

claim: Liquid sucrose intake has minimal impact on skeletal muscle in terms of both genome-wide transcriptional variance and the number of DEGs.
source: Here, we found that in contrast to the massive transcriptional regulation observed in the liver and vWAT, liquid sucrose intake has minimal impact on SkM in terms of both genome-wide transcriptional variance (Figure 3a) and the number of DEGs (Figures 3a and 4a and b).
evidence: This claim is supported by PCA and differential gene expression analysis shown in Figures 3a and 4a-b.

claim: In JNK_D1-treated skeletal muscle, a substantial quantitative difference in gene expression emerged, encompassing 4,159 (20.9%) DEGs.
source: While in JNK_D1-treated SkM, a substantial quantitative difference in gene expression emerged, encompassing 4,159 (20.9%) DEGs, of which 97% up-regulated (1552 out of 1588) and 99% down-regulated (2557 out of 2571) genes being exclusively dependent on the JNK_D1 treatment (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4a and b.

claim: 97% of up-regulated genes and 99% of down-regulated genes in JNK_D1-treated skeletal muscle were exclusively dependent on the JNK_D1 treatment.
source: While in JNK_D1-treated SkM, a substantial quantitative difference in gene expression emerged, encompassing 4,159 (20.9%) DEGs, of which 97% up-regulated (1552 out of 1588) and 99% down-regulated (2557 out of 2571) genes being exclusively dependent on the JNK_D1 treatment (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4a and b.

claim: Many of the upregulated genes in JNK_D1-treated skeletal muscle are involved in immune-related pathways, including hematopoietic cell lineage, osteoclast differentiation, chemokine signaling pathway, phagosome, and Fc gamma R-mediated phagocytosis.
source: Functional analysis revealed that many of the upregulated genes are involved in immune-related pathways, including hematopoietic cell lineage (HSCs), osteoclast differentiation, chemokine signaling pathway, phagosome, and Fc gamma R-mediated phagocytosis, and down-regulated genes are involved in OXPHOS, thermogenesis, TCA cycle, carbon metabolism, cardiac muscle contraction, and insulin signaling pathway (Figure 4c and d, Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4c and d.

claim: Down-regulated genes in JNK_D1-treated skeletal muscle are involved in OXPHOS, thermogenesis, TCA cycle, carbon metabolism, cardiac muscle contraction, and insulin signaling pathway.
source: Functional analysis revealed that many of the upregulated genes are involved in immune-related pathways, including hematopoietic cell lineage (HSCs), osteoclast differentiation, chemokine signaling pathway, phagosome, and Fc gamma R-mediated phagocytosis, and down-regulated genes are involved in OXPHOS, thermogenesis, TCA cycle, carbon metabolism, cardiac muscle contraction, and insulin signaling pathway (Figure 4c and d, Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4c and d.

claim: 86% and 69% of shared DEGs between skeletal muscle and vWAT, and the brain, exhibited consistent changes in response to JNK_D1 treatment.
source: Specifically, 86% and 69% of shared DEGs between SkM and vWAT, and the brain, exhibited consistent changes in response to JNK_D1 treatment (the same log2FC sign, indicating either upregulated or downregulated in both tissues being compared), with a Spearman correlation of 0.78 and 0.54, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of log2FC values between tissues.

claim: Shared DEGs between skeletal muscle and vWAT after JNK_D1 treatment were found to be involved in several critical metabolic processes, including cholesterol metabolism, bile acid biosynthesis and secretion, and regulation of energy homeostasis.
source: These shared DEGs were found to be involved in several critical metabolic processes, including cholesterol metabolism, bile acid biosynthesis and secretion (such as Lipc, Apob, Slc7a1, Angptl3, Slc10a1), and regulation of energy homeostasis (e.g. Lep), suggesting that SkM had a major metabolic adaptation to JNK_D1 treatment and exerts its metabolic effect, at least partially, through coordinated interactions with other tissues.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the functional annotation of shared DEGs and their known roles in metabolism.

claim: Skeletal muscle had a major metabolic adaptation to JNK_D1 treatment and exerts its metabolic effect, at least partially, through coordinated interactions with other tissues.
source: These shared DEGs were found to be involved in several critical metabolic processes, including cholesterol metabolism, bile acid biosynthesis and secretion (such as Lipc, Apob, Slc7a1, Angptl3, Slc10a1), and regulation of energy homeostasis (e.g. Lep), suggesting that SkM had a major metabolic adaptation to JNK_D1 treatment and exerts its metabolic effect, at least partially, through coordinated interactions with other tissues.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the analysis of shared DEGs and their correlation across tissues.

claim: The intervention with sucrose-sweetened water triggered extensive transcriptional changes in the liver and adipose tissues, including those involved in fatty acid and oxidative metabolism.
source: By studying the hepatic and extrahepatic tissues using genome-wide transcriptome data and integrative analyses with GEMs, we found that the intervention with sucrose-sweetened water triggered extensive transcriptional changes in the liver and adipose tissues, including those involved in fatty acid and oxidative metabolism.
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptomic analysis and genome-scale metabolic modeling.

claim: Upon chronic overnutrition, adipose lipogenesis is significantly downregulated, which leads to ectopic lipid accumulation and insulin resistance.
source: It has been reported that upon chronic overnutrition, adipose lipogenesis is significantly downregulated, which leads to ectopic lipid accumulation and insulin resistance (Jeon et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jeon et al., 2023.

claim: In the sucrose-sweetened water group, the mRNA expression of many genes related to fatty acid metabolism and uptake is downregulated in adipose tissue.
source: In line with this, we found that in the sucrose-sweetened water group, the mRNA expression of many genes related to fatty acid metabolism and uptake is downregulated in adipose tissue.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis of adipose tissue.

claim: Genes related to fatty acid metabolism and uptake showed opposite regulation between liver and adipose tissue in response to diet intervention.
source: Interestingly, those genes showed the opposite regulation between liver and adipose tissue, indicating their complementary role in these metabolic processes in response to the diet intervention.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of gene expression patterns between liver and adipose tissue.

claim: JNK-IN-5A, especially when administered at a regular dosage (JNK_D1, 30 mg/kg/d), effectively opposite a substantial portion of the transcriptional changes induced by sucrose consumption.
source: Our data demonstrated that JNK-IN-5A, especially when administered at a regular dosage (JNK_D1, 30 mg/kg/d), effectively opposite a substantial portion of the transcriptional changes induced by sucrose consumption, particularly those related to carbon, fatty acid metabolism, OXPHOS, and thermogenesis in the liver and adipose tissues.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis and pathway enrichment analysis.

claim: JNK_D1-treated skeletal muscle exhibited profound transcriptional changes related to HSCs, osteoclast differentiation, and immune-related pathways.
source: However, our study also revealed that JNK_D1-treated skeletal muscle exhibited profound transcriptional changes related to HSCs, osteoclast differentiation, and immune-related pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional enrichment analysis of DEGs in skeletal muscle.

claim: Transcriptional changes in JNK_D1-treated skeletal muscle were not confined to skeletal muscle but exhibited correlations with transcriptional changes in the liver, adipose tissue, and brain tissue.
source: Importantly, we found that these changes were not confined to skeletal muscle but exhibited correlations with transcriptional changes in the liver, adipose tissue, and even brain tissue.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of log2FC values between tissues.

claim: The JNK pathway regulates HSCs expansion and self-renewal in JNK-IN-8-treated CD34+CD45RA-CB cells.
source: Previously, Xiao et al., 2019 demonstrated that the JNK pathway regulates HSCs expansion and self-renewal in JNK-IN-8-treated CD34+CD45RA-CB cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Xiao et al., 2019.

claim: Mice with muscle-specific JNK1/2 knockout have a muscle phenotype that mimics that of endurance-trained athletes.
source: Lessard et al., 2018 demonstrated that mice with muscle-specific JNK1/2 knockout, have a muscle phenotype that mimics that of endurance-trained athletes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lessard et al., 2018.

claim: Long-term JNK inhibition may disrupt liver regeneration, as JNK plays a critical role in liver repair by regulating hepatocyte proliferation and survival following injury or stress.
source: For instance, long-term JNK inhibition may disrupt liver regeneration, as JNK plays a critical role in liver repair by regulating hepatocyte proliferation and survival following injury or stress (Papa and Bubici, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Papa and Bubici, 2018 and represents a potential risk of JNK inhibition.

claim: In HCC, JNK acts as both a tumor promoter, driving inflammation, fibrosis, and metabolic dysregulation, and a tumor suppressor, facilitating apoptosis and cell cycle arrest in damaged hepatocytes.
source: In HCC, it has been reported that JNK acts as both a tumor promoter, driving inflammation, fibrosis, and metabolic dysregulation, and a tumor suppressor, facilitating apoptosis and cell cycle arrest in damaged hepatocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Seki et al., 2012 and represents established knowledge about JNK's dual role.

claim: Compass predicted that 2840 and 4170 metabolic reactions showed significantly altered activity following sucrose consumption in the liver and vWAT, respectively.
source: Specifically, Compass predicted that 2840 and 4170 metabolic reactions showed significantly altered activity (Wilcoxon test, adjusted p-value <0.05) following the sucrose consumption in the liver and vWAT, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by Compass metabolic modeling analysis.

claim: 89.2% and 88.3% of metabolic reactions altered by sucrose consumption were correspondingly reversed after JNK_D1 treatment in liver and vWAT.
source: 89.2% and 88.3% of which were correspondingly reversed after JNK_D1 treatment (Supplementary file 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by Compass metabolic modeling analysis.

claim: Altered tryptophan metabolism was observed in rats consuming 10% sucrose in drinking water, including decreased serum levels of kynurenic acid and kynurenine.
source: For example, Öztürk et al. reported altered tryptophan metabolism in rats consuming 10% sucrose in drinking water, including decreased serum levels of kynurenic acid and kynurenine (Ozturk and Eryavuz Onmaz, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ozturk and Eryavuz Onmaz, 2022.

claim: Increased triglyceride-bound oleate, palmitate, and stearate were observed in the livers of rats fed a 10% sucrose solution.
source: Similarly, increased triglyceride-bound oleate, palmitate, and stearate were observed in the livers of rats fed a 10% sucrose solution (Stephenson et al., 2022), indicating JNK-IN-5A treatment may regulate lipid metabolism by modulating these metabolic activities.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Stephenson et al., 2022.

claim: A total of 19,780 protein-coding genes in the rat genome were analyzed.
source: A total of 19,780 protein-coding genes in the rat genome were analyzed (Martin et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the scope of the analysis.

claim: Mapk9 is among the module members of SkM.M0.
source: Interestingly, we observed that Mapk9 is among the module members of SkM.M0, indicating a potential metabolic link coordinated by JNK inhibition, connecting SkM with other tissues, including the liver and vWAT (Figure 6b, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene co-expression network analysis shown in Figure 6b.

claim: There is a significant correlation between SkM.M0 and Liver.M0 (R = 0.67, padj = 0.006).
source: Our analysis revealed a significant correlation between SkM.M0 and Liver.M0 (R = 0.67, padj = 0.006) as well as vWAT.M3 (R = 0.58, padj = 0.03) (Figure 6b and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of module eigengenes shown in Figure 6b and c.

claim: There is a significant correlation between SkM.M0 and vWAT.M3 (R = 0.58, padj = 0.03).
source: Our analysis revealed a significant correlation between SkM.M0 and Liver.M0 (R = 0.67, padj = 0.006) as well as vWAT.M3 (R = 0.58, padj = 0.03) (Figure 6b and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of module eigengenes shown in Figure 6b and c.
